newsitem.title: CHINA: China vows to battle poverty with more funds.
newsitem.headline: China vows to battle poverty with more funds.

text.p: The Chinese government, alarmed that millions of destitute could threaten its grip on power, has vowed to "gnaw the hard bone" of poverty by pouring more funds into eliminating the problem by the turn of the century.

"In the next five years, no matter how difficult the mission to eliminate poverty...we must be resolute on winning this battle," the official People's Daily on Tuesday quoted Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin as saying.
"We must gnaw this hard bone," Jiang told a joint party and government working conference to eliminate poverty on Monday, comparing destitution to a bone.

China reduced the number of people living in poverty by five million in 1995, but about 65 million people are still struggling to get by with incomes under the official absolute poverty line of 530 yuan ($64) a year, officials say.
The central government would increase by 1.5 billion yuan ($181 million) annually the amount it allocates to fight destitution, the official Xinhua news agency said.
The funds would be used to build roads and water facilities in impoverished areas, it said.
An additional three billion yuan ($361 million) in loans would be granted annually to back profitable ventures in farming and livestock raising, Xinhua said.
Currently, the central government earmarks 10.8 billion yuan ($1.3 billion) for poverty relief annually.
Provincial governments have been asked to match 30-50 percent of the central government's outlay on the anti-poverty drive, the agency said.

Almost two decades of economic reforms introduced by paramount leader Deng Xiaoping have enabled some to get rich faster than others. Many in coastal provinces in the east have become wealthy but many in interior provinces in the west remain impoverished.
Beijing fears that the widening gap between the rich and the poor could spark social unrest and undermine its grip on power.
"Accelerating the pace of development of impoverished areas is not only an economic problem, but also a political problem which concerns the nation's long-term stability," Jiang said.

"It is an important task that is connected with running the country well and giving neighbours peace and security," he said. "Our goal of eliminating poverty by the end of the century must never be shaken."
Jiang, moving to shore up his political position, has also declared war on crime, corruption and inflation -- issues the people are most concerned about.
The communists swept to power in 1949 riding on public resentment against widespread poverty and corruption.
During an inspection tour of some of China's poorest regions earlier this month, Jiang tried to resurrect communist revolutionary fervour to fight poverty.

Jiang exhorted villagers and officials to resurrect the "glorious tradition" of the revolution that won a civil war for the communists. Revolutionary fervour died after almost two decades of economic reforms which set people free to get rich.
